transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well, I guess what brings me in is... I got really worked up in a staff meeting recently. I just started acting out this whole fall-prevention drill right there in the room, moving chairs around and waving my arms everywhere to show them. And I just... I couldn't seem to stop, even when folks were telling me to sit down. So, that's why I'm here.
Have you been feeling unusually high, energized, or excited lately?

Yeah, I have. There are these stretches where I feel... I don't know, just really bright and fired up. Like everything is finally lining up for me. But then... if someone tries to slow me down, or if they question what I'm doing, I just snap. I end up snapping at them a lot harder than I mean to.
Do these energized, irritable periods come in distinct episodes that are different from your usual self?

I'm not really sure about that. I haven't really noticed if it's a distinct... episode, I guess. I just know it happens. It's hard to say if it's completely different from my usual self or just me having a really intense few days. I don't really track when it starts and stops, so I couldn't tell you for sure.
Have you ever had a period when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I have days where I feel a bit down or tired, sure, but... not like that. Not every day for two straight weeks. It's mostly just those times I get really fired up, like I said.
During these fired-up times, have you ever heard or seen things that other people couldn't?

Yeah, actually. When I was in those fired-up stretches... you know, when I'm sleeping only a few hours a night and making all these big plans... I was hearing things. Like, I'd hear calls that just weren't there. And at the same time, I was feeling completely sure that my supervisor at work was setting traps for me. It just felt really real at the time.
Have you ever heard those calls or felt sure your supervisor was setting traps for you when you were not in one of those fired-up periods?

Yeah, I have. Um... there was this one calmer stretch I remember. I was sleeping more normally, getting regular rest, and I wasn't rushing around with all those projects. Just feeling kind of regular. 

But even then, for several weeks, I still heard my name being called out when no one was there. And I stayed completely convinced that people at work were keeping notes on me. So, yeah, it didn't just happen when I was all fired up.
Have you ever had a stretch of feeling unusually energized or irritable that lasted at least one full week?

Yeah, definitely. I've had stretches like that. I'll feel really bright and... just fired up, you know? Like everything is finally lining up perfectly and I have all this energy. But then, if someone tries to slow me down or questions what I'm doing, I get really irritable. I'll just snap at them, a lot harder than I mean to. And that can go on for a week or more at a time.
When you were feeling otherwise regular, did the voices or beliefs about people at work continue for at least two weeks?

Yeah, it did. Like I was saying a minute ago, it went on for several weeks. I was in that calmer stretch... sleeping normal, not rushing around with all those projects. Just feeling regular. But for that whole time—definitely longer than two weeks—I was still hearing my name being called out, and I stayed completely convinced that people at work were keeping notes on me.
About how long has this whole problem been going on, from when it first started until now?

Well, it's been going on for about a year and five months now. It all kind of started when we got a new supervisor. He started criticizing my work right off the bat, and then he started taking away these briefings I used to lead. That's when everything really started.

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with schizoaffective disorder, manic type: the patient has clear manic episodes lasting at least one week with elevated/expansive energy, irritability, decreased need for sleep, increased activity, and impaired behavior, along with psychotic symptoms. Crucially, hallucinations and persecutory delusions also persisted for several weeks during a period described as otherwise regular and non-manic, satisfying the requirement for psychosis outside mood episodes. There is no evidence of a major depressive episode, supporting the manic type.
